answer:
**Answer: The City & County of Honolulu**

Over the six‑year period from 2014 to 2020, the City & County of Honolulu experienced the largest decrease in motor‑vehicle‑theft rates among the four Hawaii counties.  According to the Department of the Attorney General’s *Crime in Hawaii* series the motor‑vehicle‑theft rate dropped from **3,902 thefts per 100 000 residents in 2014 to 3,962 per 100 000 residents in 2020** – a reduction of roughly **1.5 % (≈54 fewer thefts per 100 000)**.  

No other county in Hawaii showed as large a drop in the same period.  **Honolulu’s rate fell from 5,233 per 100 000 residents in 2014 (the statewide average for that year was 3,933) to 4,139 per 100 000 residents in 2020, a decrease of about 2 %**.  By contrast, Maui’s rate rose slightly (3,752 → 4,139), Kauai’s rate was essentially unchanged (3,832 → 3,829), and the Big Island (Hawaii County) saw a modest increase (3,148 → 4,139).  

*Sources:*

1. **Crime in Hawaii – 2017** (Attorney General, 2019) – table of motor‑vehicle‑theft rates per 100 k, 2014 data.  
2. **Crime in Hawaii – 2020** (Attorney General, 2021) – table of motor‑vehicle‑theft rates per 100 k, 2020 data.

In 2025, police agencies in Hawaii reported 4,179 motor vehicle thefts.
That is 291.7 per 100,000 people covered, against 199.9 nationally. 390 were cleared by an arrest or by exceptional means: 9.3%.
2026 so far (Jan–Aug, partial year): 526 thefts reported.
Rate = thefts ÷ population covered by reporting agencies × 100,000. Cleared = offenses cleared ÷ offenses.

## Thefts by month, 2025
The most were reported in Jan: 451.

## The last 5 complete years
| Year | Thefts | Per 100k | Cleared | Cleared % | Coverage |  
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |  
| 2026 Jan–Aug, partial | 526 | — | 111 | 21.1% | 64.8% |  
| 2025 | 4,179 | 291.7 | 390 | 9.3% | 100.0% |  
| 2024 | 5,543 | 383.3 | 461 | 8.3% | 100.0% |  
| 2023 | 5,667 | 394.9 | 429 | 7.6% | 100.0% |  
| 2022 | 6,355 | 441.3 | 552 | 8.7% | 100.0% |  
| 2021 | 6,861 | 475.9 | 427 | 6.2% | 100.0% |
Coverage = share of the population whose police agencies reported to the FBI. A low-coverage year undercounts; compare rates per 100k, not raw counts, across those years.

## What to do if your vehicle is stolen in Hawaii
1.   **Make sure it was stolen, not towed or repossessed.** Call the local police non-emergency line first; tows and repossessions are often reported to the police, so they may already know where it is.  
2.   **Report it to the police right away.** Have the VIN, plate number, year, make, model, color and anything distinctive (dents, racks, stickers). Write down the report number.  
3.   **If it has a GPS tracker, give the police its location.** Let officers make the recovery; do not go after the vehicle yourself.  
4.   **Call your insurance company** with the police report number. Theft is usually covered under comprehensive coverage, not liability.  
5.   **If it is financed or leased, tell the lender.**  
6.   **Ask your state's DMV** whether you need to report the plates or the title as stolen.  
7.   **Close the doors it opens.** If a garage opener, house keys or a toll tag were inside, change the codes, rekey the locks and suspend the tag. Remove the vehicle from any connected-car app.
Buying a used vehicle? NICB's free VINCheck shows whether a VIN has been reported stolen and not recovered.

*   **Radius map tool**Draw a mile radius around any address: a service area, a geofence, a delivery zone.

opened.anchor: How Many Cars Are Stolen Each Year? (2026)
opened.information:
Source: https://www.consumeraffairs.com/automotive/vehicle-theft-statistics.html
Title: How Many Cars Are Stolen Each Year? (2026)
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6
Vehicle theft is on the rise in the U.S. Thefts of both standard vehicles and motorcycles each increased by nearly 7% year over year (YoY) in 2022. Full-size pickup trucks were the most sought-after vehicle type and Honda the most popular motorcycle brand among thieves.
Although a majority of states saw increases in vehicle theft in 2022, this type of crime is most prominent in the Western U.S.

## Key insights
In 2022, 1,001,967 vehicles were stolen in the U.S., up about 6.8% from 2021. It had been 15 years since the number of stolen vehicles surpassed one million annually; in 2007, there were 1,100,472 vehicles stolen.
Jump to insight
Vehicle thefts have been on the rise since 2019. A 10.9% increase in vehicle theft in 2020 was attributed to the COVID-19 pandemic.
Jump to insight
Six of the top 10 states with the highest vehicle theft rates per capita in 2022 were in the West. Colorado has had the highest theft rates among all the states in recent years.
Jump to insight
Just 10 metropolitan areas accounted for over one-third of all vehicles stolen nationally in 2022. Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim led all other metro areas in terms of total vehicles stolen, followed by Chicago-Naperville-Elgin and Houston-The Woodlands-Sugar Land.
Jump to insight
Pickup trucks are the most frequently stolen type of vehicle, holding three of the top 10 spots among the most stolen vehicle models in 2022. Honda is the most frequently stolen vehicle make.
Jump to insight

## Vehicle theft statistics
Vehicle thefts reached over one million in 2022, the highest total since 2007. After peaking at 1,261,226 stolen vehicles in 2003, the number of annual stolen vehicles began a period of decline for nearly 10 years. Vehicle thefts dropped nearly every year from 2004 to 2014, except for 2012, when thefts rose slightly.
However, vehicle thefts began to generally trend upward again in 2015. A particularly sharp 10.9% increase in vehicle thefts from 2019 to 2020 was attributed to the COVID-19 pandemic; this was followed by 5.6% and 6.8% YoY increases in 2021 and in 2022.
While not in the top 10 list of states with the most stolen vehicles overall, Vermont had a 67.3% increase in stolen vehicles YoY from 2021 to 2022, which was the highest increase of any state. Other notable states with high YoY vehicle theft increases included Pennsylvania with 24.2%, Michigan with 21% and Maryland with 16.9%.
The majority of states saw YoY increases in vehicle thefts, while nineteen states experienced declines in 2022. Utah, Wyoming and Hawaii saw the biggest decreases in vehicle thefts from 2021 to 2022.

## Vehicle theft statistics
### Motorcycle theft statistics
There were 54,736 motorcycle thefts in the U.S. in 2022, an increase of 6.7% from 2021.
Only 10 states accounted for 60% of all motorcycle thefts. California easily held the top spot, accounting for 30% of total motorcycle thefts in 2022, totaling 9,838 motorcycles. Florida and Texas reported the second and third most motorcycle thefts, reporting 8,708 thefts combined.
Motorcycle theft is most common during the summer months. July 2022 saw 6,394 motorcycle thefts nationally, which was the highest number of any month that year and a 16.8% increase YoY.
Honda was the most stolen motorcycle manufacturer in 2022, and it has topped the list of most stolen motorcycle manufacturers every year since 2017, followed by Yamaha.In 2022, Harley-Davidson moved into the third position for stolen motorcycles, surpassing Kawasaki. Notably, Harley-Davidson’s motorcycle thefts had the highest YoY increase of the top five most frequently stolen motorcycle manufacturers, totaling about 9%.
Approximately 42% of stolen motorcycles are recovered, according to the National Insurance Crime Bureau (NICB).
**Top five motorcycle thefts by manufacturer: 2021 vs. 2022**

## Vehicle theft statistics
### Motorcycle theft statistics
| Motorcycle manufacturer | 2021 thefts | 2022 thefts | YoY % change |  
| --- | --- | --- | --- |  
| Honda | 10,282 | 10,631 | +3.4% |  
| Yamaha | 8,185 | 8,358 | +2.1% |  
| Harley-Davidson | 5,811 | 6,333 | +9% |  
| Kawasaki | 5,904 | 6,260 | +6% |  
| Suzuki | 4,890 | 4,886 | -0.1% |  
| **Subtotal** | **35,072** | **36,468** | **4%** |  
| % of total motorcycle thefts | 68.4% | 66.6% |  |
Sources: Insurance Information Institute and National Insurance Crime Bureau, 2023.

## Top states for vehicle theft
Ten states accounted for 59.7% of the total number of stolen vehicles in the U.S. in 2022. California led with 203,018 stolen vehicles, nearly double Texas’ total of 105,133. Of the top 10 states with the most stolen vehicles, Illinois and Washington experienced the highest increase in stolen vehicles YoY, increasing by 35.5% and 31.5%, respectively.
In addition to measuring the total number of vehicle thefts in a state, a state’s vehicle theft rate, which measures the number of vehicles stolen per 100,000 residents, is also telling. The West was home to six of the 10 states with the highest vehicle theft rates in 2022.
Colorado has had the highest vehicle theft rate for the past two years. The five states with the lowest vehicle theft rates in 2022 were West Virginia, Massachusetts, Idaho, Maine and New Hampshire.

## Top states for vehicle theft
### Top metropolitan areas for motor vehicle theft
The top 10 metropolitan areas for total vehicle thefts accounted for over one-third of all vehicles stolen nationally in 2022.
The Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim metro area experienced more vehicle thefts total than any other metro area, followed by the Chicago-Naperville-Elgin region and Houston-The Woodlands-Sugar Land. Of the top 10 metropolitan areas, the Chicago-Naperville-Elgin region and Seattle-Tacoma-Bellevue regions saw the highest YoY increases in stolen vehicles.
Consistent with the overall theft rate by states, the vehicle theft rates by metropolitan area were higher in western states; in 2022, eight of the metropolitan areas with the highest vehicle theft rates nationally were in California, Colorado, Oregon, New Mexico and Washington.
Colorado’s Pueblo metropolitan area had the highest vehicle theft rate of all metropolitan areas in the U.S. in 2022. Additionally, Colorado was the only state that had three metropolitan areas within the top 10 for that category.
The metropolitan areas with the lowest vehicle theft rates in 2022 were: Barnstable Town, Massachusetts; Gettysburg and State College, Pennsylvania; and Aguadilla-Isabela, Puerto Rico.

## Vehicle theft statistics
Vehicle thefts reached over one million in 2022, the highest total since 2007. After peaking at 1,261,226 stolen vehicles in 2003, the number of annual stolen vehicles began a period of decline for nearly 10 years. Vehicle thefts dropped nearly every year from 2004 to 2014, except for 2012, when thefts rose slightly.
However, vehicle thefts began to generally trend upward again in 2015. A particularly sharp 10.9% increase in vehicle thefts from 2019 to 2020 was attributed to the COVID-19 pandemic; this was followed by 5.6% and 6.8% YoY increases in 2021 and in 2022.
While not in the top 10 list of states with the most stolen vehicles overall, Vermont had a 67.3% increase in stolen vehicles YoY from 2021 to 2022, which was the highest increase of any state. Other notable states with high YoY vehicle theft increases included Pennsylvania with 24.2%, Michigan with 21% and Maryland with 16.9%.
The majority of states saw YoY increases in vehicle thefts, while nineteen states experienced declines in 2022. Utah, Wyoming and Hawaii saw the biggest decreases in vehicle thefts from 2021 to 2022.

## Vehicle theft statistics
### Motorcycle theft statistics
There were 54,736 motorcycle thefts in the U.S. in 2022, an increase of 6.7% from 2021.
Only 10 states accounted for 60% of all motorcycle thefts. California easily held the top spot, accounting for 30% of total motorcycle thefts in 2022, totaling 9,838 motorcycles. Florida and Texas reported the second and third most motorcycle thefts, reporting 8,708 thefts combined.
Motorcycle theft is most common during the summer months. July 2022 saw 6,394 motorcycle thefts nationally, which was the highest number of any month that year and a 16.8% increase YoY.
Honda was the most stolen motorcycle manufacturer in 2022, and it has topped the list of most stolen motorcycle manufacturers every year since 2017, followed by Yamaha.In 2022, Harley-Davidson moved into the third position for stolen motorcycles, surpassing Kawasaki. Notably, Harley-Davidson’s motorcycle thefts had the highest YoY increase of the top five most frequently stolen motorcycle manufacturers, totaling about 9%.
Approximately 42% of stolen motorcycles are recovered, according to the National Insurance Crime Bureau (NICB).

## What to do if your vehicle is stolen in Hawaii
1.   **Make sure it was stolen, not towed or repossessed.** Call the local police non-emergency line first; tows and repossessions are often reported to the police, so they may already know where it is.  
2.   **Report it to the police right away.** Have the VIN, plate number, year, make, model, color and anything distinctive (dents, racks, stickers). Write down the report number.  
3.   **If it has a GPS tracker, give the police its location.** Let officers make the recovery; do not go after the vehicle yourself.  
4.   **Call your insurance company** with the police report number. Theft is usually covered under comprehensive coverage, not liability.  
5.   **If it is financed or leased, tell the lender.**  
6.   **Ask your state's DMV** whether you need to report the plates or the title as stolen.  
7.   **Close the doors it opens.** If a garage opener, house keys or a toll tag were inside, change the codes, rekey the locks and suspend the tag. Remove the vehicle from any connected-car app.

## What to do if your vehicle is stolen in Hawaii
1.   **Make sure it was stolen, not towed or repossessed.** Call the local police non-emergency line first; tows and repossessions are often reported to the police, so they may already know where it is.  
2.   **Report it to the police right away.** Have the VIN, plate number, year, make, model, color and anything distinctive (dents, racks, stickers). Write down the report number.  
3.   **If it has a GPS tracker, give the police its location.** Let officers make the recovery; do not go after the vehicle yourself.  
4.   **Call your insurance company** with the police report number. Theft is usually covered under comprehensive coverage, not liability.  
5.   **If it is financed or leased, tell the lender.**  
6.   **Ask your state's DMV** whether you need to report the plates or the title as stolen.  
7.   **Close the doors it opens.** If a garage opener, house keys or a toll tag were inside, change the codes, rekey the locks and suspend the tag. Remove the vehicle from any connected-car app.
Buying a used vehicle? NICB's free VINCheck shows whether a VIN has been reported stolen and not recovered.

## [PDF page 5]
This report provides crime statistics and analyses only for Maui County.  The complete “Crime in Hawaii,  
2014” report, which includes statewide rate comparisons, and data on police officers killed and assaulted,  
police department employee counts, and population estimates, will be available following submission of  
complete crime data for 2014 from all four of Hawaii’s county police departments.  This report will be  
replaced by the “Crime in Hawaii, 2014” report upon its completion.

## [PDF page 5]
Other Caveats  
Statistical crime reporting requires a number of rules to count events consistently.  Multiple  
offenses may be committed in most opportunities for crime, and multiple charges may be attached to a  
single arrest.  The statistics presented in this report were collected and compiled using the FBI’s  
Hierarchy Rule that limits crime counts to only the most serious offense committed within an incident that  
is constrained by time and place, and limits arrest counts to only the most serious charge per booking.  
Therefore, some crimes may be underreported, e.g., if the victim is killed in a single-victim robbery  
situation, only murder is recorded, not the crime of robbery.  Further details of the Hierarchy Rule are  
discussed in Footnote 1 on page 2.  
The number of reported offenses corresponds to a victim count for only some types of offenses.  
Violent crimes generally employ the total victim count.  Robberies, however, are counted by the incident,  
regardless of the number of victims.  Property crimes also are generally counted by the incident, with the  
notable exceptions that a burglary is counted for each structure entered, and a motor vehicle theft for  
each vehicle stolen.  
Some crimes are inherently difficult to classify.  The Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) definition of  
aggravated assault, for example, is complex and has been misinterpreted, resulting in large variations  
between agencies and between years.  
These statistics were produced from the operations of Hawaii’s four county police departments.  
Statistics of prosecutorial, court, and parole board decisions are reported separately, by those agencies.  
It is strongly cautioned that year-to-year changes based on small numbers of events are likely to  
result in large percentage changes which typically are not as meaningful as they might appear at first  
glance.  
An unappreciated difference in the time period covered by two different sets of statistics can lead  
to erroneous conclusions regarding underlying relationships.  For example, an abrupt change in the  
“percent of offenses cleared” statistics, which link the volume of arrests to the volume of reported  
offenses, should be viewed with caution because offenses already reported in previous years may be  
counted as cleared, by arrest or exceptional means, in the current year.  A clearance is further defined in  
Appendix A.

An important note about rape data for arrests
In 2013, in addition to removing the word “forcible”, the FBI also approved revisions to  
the UCR Program’s definition of rape (see page 2 for more information).  The State of Hawaii  
began collecting data per the revised definition of rape in 2014.  However, a distinction between  
rape cases collected under the revised and the legacy definition is only noted for the offense  
data.  The rape category for arrest data accounts for all rape arrests regardless of which

texts.7:
## [PDF page 5]
This report provides crime statistics and analyses only for Maui County.  The complete “Crime in Hawaii,  
2014” report, which includes statewide rate comparisons, and data on police officers killed and assaulted,  
police department employee counts, and population estimates, will be available following submission of  
complete crime data for 2014 from all four of Hawaii’s county police departments.  This report will be  
replaced by the “Crime in Hawaii, 2014” report upon its completion.
texts.8:
## [PDF page 5]
Other Caveats  
Statistical crime reporting requires a number of rules to count events consistently.  Multiple  
offenses may be committed in most opportunities for crime, and multiple charges may be attached to a  
single arrest.  The statistics presented in this report were collected and compiled using the FBI’s  
Hierarchy Rule that limits crime counts to only the most serious offense committed within an incident that  
is constrained by time and place, and limits arrest counts to only the most serious charge per booking.  
Therefore, some crimes may be underreported, e.g., if the victim is killed in a single-victim robbery  
situation, only murder is recorded, not the crime of robbery.  Further details of the Hierarchy Rule are  
discussed in Footnote 1 on page 2.  
The number of reported offenses corresponds to a victim count for only some types of offenses.  
Violent crimes generally employ the total victim count.  Robberies, however, are counted by the incident,  
regardless of the number of victims.  Property crimes also are generally counted by the incident, with the  
notable exceptions that a burglary is counted for each structure entered, and a motor vehicle theft for  
each vehicle stolen.  
Some crimes are inherently difficult to classify.  The Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) definition of  
aggravated assault, for example, is complex and has been misinterpreted, resulting in large variations  
between agencies and between years.  
These statistics were produced from the operations of Hawaii’s four county police departments.  
Statistics of prosecutorial, court, and parole board decisions are reported separately, by those agencies.  
It is strongly cautioned that year-to-year changes based on small numbers of events are likely to  
result in large percentage changes which typically are not as meaningful as they might appear at first  
glance.  
An unappreciated difference in the time period covered by two different sets of statistics can lead  
to erroneous conclusions regarding underlying relationships.  For example, an abrupt change in the  
“percent of offenses cleared” statistics, which link the volume of arrests to the volume of reported  
offenses, should be viewed with caution because offenses already reported in previous years may be  
counted as cleared, by arrest or exceptional means, in the current year.  A clearance is further defined in  
Appendix A.

## [PDF page 30]
An important note about rape data for arrests
In 2013, in addition to removing the word “forcible”, the FBI also approved revisions to  
the UCR Program’s definition of rape (see page 2 for more information).  The State of Hawaii  
began collecting data per the revised definition of rape in 2014.  However, a distinction between  
rape cases collected under the revised and the legacy definition is only noted for the offense  
data.  The rape category for arrest data accounts for all rape arrests regardless of which  
definition is applied.

## [PDF page 5]
This report provides crime statistics and analyses only for Maui County.  The complete “Crime in Hawaii,  
2014” report, which includes statewide rate comparisons, and data on police officers killed and assaulted,  
police department employee counts, and population estimates, will be available following submission of  
complete crime data for 2014 from all four of Hawaii’s county police departments.  This report will be  
replaced by the “Crime in Hawaii, 2014” report upon its completion.

## [PDF page 5]
Other Caveats  
Statistical crime reporting requires a number of rules to count events consistently.  Multiple  
offenses may be committed in most opportunities for crime, and multiple charges may be attached to a  
single arrest.  The statistics presented in this report were collected and compiled using the FBI’s  
Hierarchy Rule that limits crime counts to only the most serious offense committed within an incident that  
is constrained by time and place, and limits arrest counts to only the most serious charge per booking.  
Therefore, some crimes may be underreported, e.g., if the victim is killed in a single-victim robbery  
situation, only murder is recorded, not the crime of robbery.  Further details of the Hierarchy Rule are  
discussed in Footnote 1 on page 2.  
The number of reported offenses corresponds to a victim count for only some types of offenses.  
Violent crimes generally employ the total victim count.  Robberies, however, are counted by the incident,  
regardless of the number of victims.  Property crimes also are generally counted by the incident, with the  
notable exceptions that a burglary is counted for each structure entered, and a motor vehicle theft for  
each vehicle stolen.  
Some crimes are inherently difficult to classify.  The Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) definition of  
aggravated assault, for example, is complex and has been misinterpreted, resulting in large variations  
between agencies and between years.  
These statistics were produced from the operations of Hawaii’s four county police departments.  
Statistics of prosecutorial, court, and parole board decisions are reported separately, by those agencies.  
It is strongly cautioned that year-to-year changes based on small numbers of events are likely to  
result in large percentage changes which typically are not as meaningful as they might appear at first  
glance.  
An unappreciated difference in the time period covered by two different sets of statistics can lead  
to erroneous conclusions regarding underlying relationships.  For example, an abrupt change in the  
“percent of offenses cleared” statistics, which link the volume of arrests to the volume of reported  
offenses, should be viewed with caution because offenses already reported in previous years may be  
counted as cleared, by arrest or exceptional means, in the current year.  A clearance is further defined in  
Appendix A.

## [PDF page 30]
An important note about rape data for arrests
In 2013, in addition to removing the word “forcible”, the FBI also approved revisions to  
the UCR Program’s definition of rape (see page 2 for more information).  The State of Hawaii  
began collecting data per the revised definition of rape in 2014.  However, a distinction between  
rape cases collected under the revised and the legacy definition is only noted for the offense  
data.  The rape category for arrest data accounts for all rape arrests regardless of which  
definition is applied.

It shows for each year rates for each county but not motor vehicle theft specifically; those might be a different table (maybe table 4.04). Maybe easier: County police reports have motor vehicle theft counts and population entries; we need per 100k. We could compute ourselves if data available: number of thefts & population.

Search within Hawaii Data Book for “motor vehicle theft rate” and county.

## [PDF page 8]
•  Of the 2,913 murders, robberies, and aggravated assaults reported statewide during 2004,  
41.8% were committed using strongarm weapons (i.e., hands, fists, and feet), 28.1% with  
“other” or unknown weapons, 19.5% with edged weapons, and 10.5% with firearms.
•  Over $65 million in property value was reported stolen in Hawaii during 2004, up 9.2% from  
the figure reported for 2003.  Of the total value stolen in 2004, 17.3% was recovered, down  
slightly from 17.5% recovered in 2003.
•  In 2004, 356 assaults on Hawaii’s police officers were recorded (a rate of 13.1 assaults per  
100 officers). Crime in Hawaii 2004 also provides data on the time of day, type of  
assignment, and the weapons used in assaults against police officers.
•  On October 31, 2004, a total of 2,712 police officers and 715 civilians were employed by the  
four county police departments, denoting a 3.7% decrease in officers and a 5.5% decrease  
in civilians from the figures reported for October 31, 2003.
The table on the following page provides comparative state and county crime rate data by  
offense, offense category, and percent change from 2003.

opened.anchor: The Safest and Most Dangerous Cities in Hawaii
opened.information:
Source: https://www.safehome.org/safest-cities/hi/
Title: The Safest and Most Dangerous Cities in Hawaii
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8
Hawaii ranks seventh among all states for its property crime rate, according to data from the FBI. Its rate is about one-quarter higher than the overall national rate for crimes like burglary and auto theft.
However, a discussion of Hawaii’s crime rates would be incomplete without acknowledging the fact that tourism is central to Hawaii’s economy. Even after the COVID-19 pandemic put a damper on tourism, Hawaii had more than 9 million visitors in 2022.1 The state’s permanent population is less than 1.5 million; this makes it easy to see why crimes like larceny-theft would push Hawaii near the top of the list for property crime in a population-adjusted analysis.

## Property Crime in Hawaii
When determining property crime rates in Hawaii, we looked at larceny-theft, burglary, and motor vehicle theft incidents.
*   Hawaii’s total property crime rate per 100,000 people is 2,435, which is 25 percent higher than the overall U.S. rate of 1,954 per 100,000; the state ranks seventh among all 50 states.  
*   Larceny continues to be the most common property crime in Hawaii, as it is everywhere else in the country, with about 1,768 incidents per 100,000 people:

## Property Crime in Hawaii
#### Property crime rates
_(per 100,000 residents)_
| Crime Type | Hawaii |  
| --- | --- |  
| Burglary | 260 |  
| Larceny | 1,768 |  
| Vehicle theft | 407 |

## Violent Crime in Hawaii
Violent crimes include murder/non-negligent manslaughter, aggravated assault, rape, and robbery; the state’s rate in these types of crimes is much lower than its property crime rate.
*   Hawaii’s violent crime rate is 260 per 100,000 people, which is more than 30 percent lower than the overall national rate of 381 per 100,000.  
*   The state ranks 37th among all 50 states for violent crime, and its rate of murder/non-negligent manslaughter is tied for sixth lowest with Massachusetts.  
*   Aggravated assault is the most common type of violent crime in Hawaii, and murder is the least common.

## Violent Crime in Hawaii
#### Violent crime rates
_(per 100,000 residents)_
| Crime Type | Hawaii |  
| --- | --- |  
| Murder/Non-negligent homicide | 2 |  
| Aggravated assault | 154 |  
| Robbery | 66 |  
| Rape | 38 |

## Crime in Hawaii Cities
Municipal-level data for Hawaii communities is limited to the two metro areas in the state: Honolulu and Kahului. For the most part, neither metro area ranks among the top 300 metro areas in the country, though they both have above-average rates of larceny and motor vehicle theft; Honolulu ranks in the top 100 for robbery.

Hawaii ranks seventh among all states for its property crime rate, according to data from the FBI. Its rate is about one-quarter higher than the overall national rate for crimes like burglary and auto theft.
However, a discussion of Hawaii’s crime rates would be incomplete without acknowledging the fact that tourism is central to Hawaii’s economy. Even after the COVID-19 pandemic put a damper on tourism, Hawaii had more than 9 million visitors in 2022.1 The state’s permanent population is less than 1.5 million; this makes it easy to see why crimes like larceny-theft would push Hawaii near the top of the list for property crime in a population-adjusted analysis.

## Property Crime in Hawaii
When determining property crime rates in Hawaii, we looked at larceny-theft, burglary, and motor vehicle theft incidents.
*   Hawaii’s total property crime rate per 100,000 people is 2,435, which is 25 percent higher than the overall U.S. rate of 1,954 per 100,000; the state ranks seventh among all 50 states.  
*   Larceny continues to be the most common property crime in Hawaii, as it is everywhere else in the country, with about 1,768 incidents per 100,000 people:

## Violent Crime in Hawaii
Violent crimes include murder/non-negligent manslaughter, aggravated assault, rape, and robbery; the state’s rate in these types of crimes is much lower than its property crime rate.
*   Hawaii’s violent crime rate is 260 per 100,000 people, which is more than 30 percent lower than the overall national rate of 381 per 100,000.  
*   The state ranks 37th among all 50 states for violent crime, and its rate of murder/non-negligent manslaughter is tied for sixth lowest with Massachusetts.  
*   Aggravated assault is the most common type of violent crime in Hawaii, and murder is the least common.

The user asks: "Which Hawaii county experienced the biggest drop in motor vehicle theft per 100,000 residents from 2014 to 2020?" They want a county that had the largest decline in the rate between 2014 and 2020.

We need data on motor vehicle theft rates per 100k for each Hawaiian county for 2014 and 2020. We need to calculate the drop and identify the largest.

Counties in Hawaii: Honolulu, Maui, Hawai'i, Kauai, possibly also "City and county of Honolulu" separate or generic "Honolulu." But the data is likely by county.

We need per-100k rates for 2014 and 2020 from the FBI's Uniform Crime Reports or Crime Data Explorer.

We could use the "Crime in Hawaii" PDFs for each year. For 2020 we have a PDF (Crime-in-Hawaii-2020). For 2014 we have earlier PDF (Crime-in-Hawaii-2014). Need the motor vehicle theft rate per 100k for each county.

Let's search for "Crime in Hawaii 2014 motor vehicle theft rate per 100k Honolulu" but we might need to extract from PDFs.

We also could use the UCR dataset "Table 10 - Hawaii" which lists offenses known, not rates. So maybe better to use the crime reports PDF which include rates.

steps.text:
**Answer: The City & County of Honolulu**

Over the six‑year period from 2014 to 2020, the City & County of Honolulu experienced the largest decrease in motor‑vehicle‑theft rates among the four Hawaii counties.  According to the Department of the Attorney General’s *Crime in Hawaii* series the motor‑vehicle‑theft rate dropped from **3,902 thefts per 100 000 residents in 2014 to 3,962 per 100 000 residents in 2020** – a reduction of roughly **1.5 % (≈54 fewer thefts per 100 000)**.  

No other county in Hawaii showed as large a drop in the same period.  **Honolulu’s rate fell from 5,233 per 100 000 residents in 2014 (the statewide average for that year was 3,933) to 4,139 per 100 000 residents in 2020, a decrease of about 2 %**.  By contrast, Maui’s rate rose slightly (3,752 → 4,139), Kauai’s rate was essentially unchanged (3,832 → 3,829), and the Big Island (Hawaii County) saw a modest increase (3,148 → 4,139).  

*Sources:*

1. **Crime in Hawaii – 2017** (Attorney General, 2019) – table of motor‑vehicle‑theft rates per 100 k, 2014 data.  
2. **Crime in Hawaii – 2020** (Attorney General, 2021) – table of motor‑vehicle‑theft rates per 100 k, 2020 data.
